title: Heat exhaustion
summary: Tiredness, dizziness, headache, heavy sweating, and feeling sick after hot weather or hard activity in the sun. Catching it early stops it from becoming heatstroke, which is life-threatening.
steps: Move the person to a cool, shaded, well-ventilated place.
Lay them down and raise their legs slightly.
Cool the skin: sponge with cool water, fan them, apply cool wet cloths to the neck, armpits, and groin.

If they are alert and able to swallow, give sips of cool water — every 5 minutes — or an oral rehydration solution. A pinch of salt and a teaspoon of sugar in a cup of water works if nothing else is available.
Keep cooling them and monitoring for 30 minutes. They should start to feel better as they cool and rehydrate.
Rest for the rest of the day. Avoid heat and exertion until next day.
avoid: Do not give salt tablets or large salty drinks at once.
Do not give alcohol, caffeine, or very cold drinks (which may cause stomach cramps).
Do not return them to the heat or activity as soon as they feel better.
Do not assume they are fine if they remain confused or stop sweating — these are heatstroke warning signs.
whenToEscalate: Emergency immediately — treat as heatstroke — if: skin is hot and dry (sweating has stopped), temperature is high, confusion, slurred speech, seizures, vomiting, or loss of consciousness.
If symptoms do not improve within 30 minutes of cooling and rehydration.
Infants, elderly, pregnant people, and those with heart or kidney disease — see a doctor early.
Heat exhaustion in someone working in heavy clothing or PPE — extra urgent.
specialty: Emergency department for any heatstroke sign; general physician for review.
